text: MATTER means…
answers: Anything that has mass and takes up space
How hot or cold something is
To use the senses to gain knowledge
solution: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space: your squad training ball, the air inside it, even you!
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: PROPERTIES means…
answers: Characteristics used to describe or identify a substance
Anything that has mass and takes up space
How hot or cold something is
solution: Properties are traits like color, shape, texture, magnetism, and conductivity that help you tell materials apart.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: OBSERVE means…
answers: To use the senses to examine or gain knowledge
solution: Observing = using your senses (sight, touch, smell, hearing) to learn about something.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: MEASUREMENT means…
answers: The size, length, or amount of something, as established by measuring
To use the senses to gain knowledge
Anything that has mass and takes up space
How hot or cold something is
solution: A measurement is a number found by measuring, like 94 grams or 30 centimeters.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: VOLUME means…
answers: The amount of space matter takes up (mL, L, or cm³)
How hot or cold something is
solution: In science, volume is how much space something takes up, measured in milliliters, liters, or cubic centimeters.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: TEMPERATURE means…
answers: How hot or cold something is
The amount of space matter takes up
solution: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is, measured with a thermometer in °C or °F.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: STANDARD UNITS are…
answers: Units with agreed-upon values that everyone uses to measure the same thing
Units you make up, like 'shoe lengths'
Only units used in the USA
Things you observe with your senses
solution: Standard units (grams, meters, liters) mean the same thing to everyone, so results can be compared.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: MASS means…
answers: The amount of matter in an object
How hot or cold something is
How much space something takes up
solution: Mass is how much matter ("stuff") is in an object, measured in grams or kilograms.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: A SUBSTANCE is…
answers: A specific type of matter, like water, salt, or iron
solution: A substance is a particular kind of matter with its own properties.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: Which of these is NOT matter?
solution: Light is energy. It has no mass and doesn't take up space, so it isn't matter.
hint: Name the property: amount of matter, space occupied, or hot/cold.

text: What property do a steel screw, an iron nail, and a paperclip have in common?
answers: They are all soluble in water.
solution: Steel and iron are attracted to magnets. A paperclip is made of steel.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: A plain carbon-steel paperclip is recovered from a supply crate. Which set of properties best describes it?
answers: Silver, soluble in water, conductor of electricity
solution: A paperclip is steel: silver colored, magnetic, and metal conducts electricity.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: You drop a magnet into your Creative build kit. Which item will stick to it?
answers: A steel screw that fell in the bin
solution: plastic building pieces are plastic and rubber, which aren't magnetic. The steel screw is!
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: Which of these is NOT attracted to a magnet?
solution: Surprise: aluminum is a metal but it is NOT magnetic. Iron and steel are.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: How could you separate steel paperclips from a pile of sand?
solution: Magnetism! The magnet pulls out the steel paperclips and leaves the sand.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: Magnets attract objects made of…
solution: Iron and steel (and nickel) are magnetic. Aluminum and copper are metals but NOT magnetic.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: A supply rover has a steel frame and plastic wheels. Which part would stick to a magnet?
solution: Steel is magnetic; plastic and rubber aren't.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: Which list has ONLY magnetic objects?
answers: Iron nail, steel paperclip, steel screw
Aluminum foil, copper wire, steel screw
solution: Iron and steel are magnetic. Plastic, copper, aluminum, rubber, glass, and wood are not.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: Is every metal magnetic?
answers: No. Only some metals, like iron, nickel, and steel
solution: Some metals are attracted to magnets. Iron, nickel, and ordinary carbon steel are familiar examples; aluminum and copper are not.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: A student says 'all silver-colored objects are magnetic.' What's the best way to check?
answers: Hold a magnet near several silver objects, like a paperclip and aluminum foil
solution: Aluminum foil is silver but NOT magnetic, so testing proves the claim is wrong.
hint: Color and being metal do not guarantee attraction to a magnet.

text: Students want to know which objects can conduct electricity. What do they need for their investigation?
answers: A circuit and an energy source
A heat source and a magnet
A light source and a circuit
solution: To test electrical conductivity, put the object in a circuit with a battery (energy source) and see if the bulb lights.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: A material that lets electricity flow through it easily is called a…
solution: Conductors (like metals) let electricity flow.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: A material that does NOT let electricity flow through it easily is called an…
solution: Insulators (plastic, rubber, wood, glass) block electricity.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: At the Reboot Van workshop, an object completes a working battery-and-bulb test circuit. The bulb lights. What does this show about the object?
solution: If the bulb lights, electricity flowed through the object, so it's a conductor.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: Which item would make a bulb light up when placed in a circuit?
solution: Aluminum is a metal, so it conducts electricity. The others are insulators.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: Which of these is the BEST insulator of electricity?
solution: Plastic is an insulator. Metals like copper, steel, and aluminum are conductors.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: Which material is a conductor of electricity?
solution: Copper is a metal, and metals conduct electricity. That's why wires are made of copper.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: What do you need to build a simple circuit to test conductivity?
answers: A battery, wires, a bulb, and the object being tested
solution: Battery (energy source) + wires + bulb + test object = conductivity tester.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: Which part of a game controller's charging cord is the conductor?
solution: The metal wires carry the electricity. The plastic around them is an insulator.
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: A squad tests exposed graphite and dry wood in the same working circuit. Only graphite lets the bulb light. Which claim fits the evidence?
answers: Graphite is a conductor and wood is an insulator
solution: Surprise: graphite isn't a metal, but it still conducts electricity!
hint: Think about whether current can pass through the material in a working circuit.

text: What property can be investigated by exposing different materials to heat?
solution: Thermal conductivity = how well a material lets heat move through it.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: A metal spoon and a plastic spoon sit in hot cocoa. Which handle gets hot first?
answers: They heat up exactly the same
solution: Metal is a good thermal conductor; heat travels through it quickly.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Why do pots and pans often have plastic or wooden handles?
answers: Plastic and wood slow heat transfer toward the handle
They make the pan cook faster
Plastic conducts heat better than metal
solution: Plastic and wood are poor thermal conductors. They slow heat transfer compared with metal, so the handle warms more slowly.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Which material is the BEST conductor of heat?
solution: Metals like copper conduct heat really well.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: A foam cooler keeps your water cold at a island mission because foam is…
answers: A poor conductor of heat (an insulator)
solution: Foam is a thermal insulator: it slows heat from getting in.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Thermal conductivity describes…
answers: How well heat moves through a material
solution: 'Thermal' means heat. Thermal conductivity = how easily heat travels through.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: On a cold morning, a metal bleacher feels colder than a wooden bench, even though they're the same temperature. Why?
answers: Metal conducts heat away from your body faster
The metal really is a lower temperature
solution: Metal pulls heat out of your skin quickly, so it FEELS colder.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Which item is designed to be a thermal insulator?
solution: Jackets trap your body heat. The others are designed to conduct.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Equal pieces of butter sit at the same distance along equal-size metal, plastic, and wooden spoons. All spoon tips touch the same hot water. Which butter is likely to melt first?
answers: They all melt at the same time
solution: Metal is the best heat conductor, so heat reaches its butter first.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Equal ice cubes sit on same-temperature metal and plastic trays in a warm room. The ice on metal melts faster. What does this suggest?
solution: Metal moves heat from the room into the ice faster.
hint: A thermal conductor transfers heat more easily than an insulator.

text: Something that dissolves in water is described as…
solution: Soluble = dissolves (like sugar or salt in water).
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: Which of these is soluble in water?
solution: Sugar dissolves in water. Sand, plastic, and steel don't.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: You drop a foam training dart into water. It floats and doesn't dissolve. The dart is…
solution: It didn't dissolve, so it's insoluble.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: You stir a sports drink powder into water and it disappears. This shows the powder is…
solution: The powder dissolved, so it's soluble.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: Which mixture could you separate by letting the water evaporate?
solution: Salt dissolves in water. When the water evaporates, the salt is left behind.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: Two jars both have a fluffy white powder: one is flour, one is powdered sugar. Which test would help tell them apart?
answers: Stir each into water and observe which dissolves
Test each in an electric circuit
solution: Powdered sugar dissolves in water; flour doesn't really dissolve and makes the water cloudy. Same color, different solubility!
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: When salt dissolves in water, where does the salt go?
answers: It's still there, mixed in pieces too tiny to see
solution: Dissolved salt is still in the water. Taste ocean water and you'll know!
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: Which mixture can be separated with a filter (like a coffee filter)?
answers: Clear lemonade with all sugar dissolved
solution: Sand doesn't dissolve, so the filter catches it. Dissolved salt and sugar pass right through.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: Oil and water are shaken together. Minutes later, the oil floats on top. Oil is…
solution: The oil didn't dissolve, so it's insoluble.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: A supply spill contains gravel, sand, and salt. Which property helps separate the salt from both other solids?
answers: Solubility: add water, filter, then evaporate
solution: Salt dissolves; gravel and sand don't. Filter them out, then evaporate the water to get the salt back.
hint: Dissolving spreads a substance through water; it does not make the substance disappear.

text: Which tool measures the MASS of an object?
solution: A balance or scale measures mass in grams (g) or kilograms (kg).
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: Which tool measures the VOLUME of a liquid?
solution: A graduated cylinder measures liquid volume in milliliters (mL).
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: Which tool measures TEMPERATURE?
solution: A thermometer measures temperature in °C or °F.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: Which unit would you use to measure the volume of water in your water bottle?
solution: Liquid volume = milliliters or liters.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: A supply box is 10 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2 cm tall. What is its volume?
solution: Volume = length × width × height = 10 × 5 × 2 = 100 cm³.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: Which tool would you use to measure the length of a training field?
solution: Length is measured with a ruler, meter stick, or measuring tape.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: Which is an example of a NONSTANDARD unit?
solution: Pencils come in different sizes, so 'pencil lengths' isn't standard.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: A rock is dropped into a graduated cylinder. The water rises from 30 mL to 45 mL. What is the rock's volume?
solution: 45 − 30 = 15 mL. The rock pushed aside 15 mL of water.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: When reading a graduated cylinder, you should…
answers: Read at eye level at the bottom of the curved water line
Read the top edge of the curve
solution: Get eye level and read the bottom of the curve (called the meniscus).
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: An empty cup has a mass of 250 g. With water in it, the mass is 400 g. What's the mass of the water?
solution: Subtract the empty cup’s mass from the filled cup’s mass: 400 g − 250 g = 150 g of water.
hint: Match the measured property to the tool and its units.

text: What is the difference between mass and weight?
answers: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is gravity's pull on that mass
They are exactly the same thing
Weight is the amount of space something takes up
Mass changes on the Moon but weight doesn't
solution: Mass = how much stuff. Weight = how hard gravity pulls on that stuff.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: An astronaut takes a squad training ball to the Moon. What happens?
answers: Its mass stays the same, but it weighs less
Its mass and weight both stay the same
solution: The Moon has less gravity, so weight goes down, but the ball has the same amount of stuff (mass).
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: Weight is caused by…
answers: The force of gravity pulling on mass
solution: Weight = gravity's pull on mass.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: Which tool measures WEIGHT (the pull of gravity)?
solution: A spring scale stretches as gravity pulls on the object.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: Jupiter has stronger gravity than Earth. On Jupiter, your mass would ___ and your weight would ___.
answers: stay the same; stay the same
solution: Mass never changes based on location. More gravity = more weight.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: A Creative building tower is taken apart and all the bricks are put on a scale. Compared to the built tower, the mass is…
solution: Same bricks = same matter = same mass. Matter isn't lost when you take something apart.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: An ice cube has a mass of 20 g. After it melts completely, the water has a mass of… No material escapes or spills.
solution: Changing state doesn't change mass. It's the same water, just liquid now.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: 10 g of sugar is dissolved in 100 g of water. What is the total mass of the sugar water? No material escapes or spills.
solution: Dissolved sugar is still there! 100 + 10 = 110 g.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: Mass is measured in ___. Weight is measured in ___.
solution: Mass uses grams/kilograms. Weight is a force, measured in newtons (or pounds).
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: You pump air into a flat squad training ball. Its mass…
answers: Increases a tiny bit, because air has mass
solution: Air is matter, so adding air adds mass.
hint: Mass is amount of matter. Weight depends on gravity.

text: Which property can you observe just by LOOKING at something?
solution: Color is observed with your eyes. The others need tools or tests.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Rubbing your hand on a squad training ball to see if it's smooth or bumpy tests its…
solution: Texture is how something feels.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Which sense would you use to observe the TEXTURE of a material?
solution: Texture = how it feels, so touch!
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Which of these is a property of a plastic building brick?
answers: Hard, plastic, and it doesn't dissolve in water
solution: plastic building bricks are hard plastic, insoluble, nonmagnetic, and insulators.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Which word describes a material that bends easily without breaking, like a rubber band?
solution: Flexible = bends without breaking.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: A diamond can scratch glass, but glass can't scratch a diamond. This compares their…
solution: Hardness: harder materials scratch softer ones.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Light passes right through a clear window. Which property does this describe?
solution: Transparent = you can see through it.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: At the island training range, which property makes a rubber ball bouncy?
answers: Elasticity: it stretches and springs back
solution: Elastic materials like rubber squish and spring back into shape.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: TRANSLUCENT means…
answers: Some light passes through, but you can't see clearly (like wax paper)
solution: Translucent is in between transparent and opaque.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Why should you NEVER taste unknown substances during a science investigation?
answers: They could be harmful; use other safe tests instead
Tasting is the most accurate test
Taste isn't one of the senses
solution: Safety first! Scientists observe with sight, touch, and careful tests, not taste.
hint: Use the property described in the observation.

text: Which state of matter has a definite shape AND definite volume?
solution: Solids (like a plastic building brick) keep their shape and volume.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume?
solution: Liquids flow to fit the container, but the amount stays the same.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: Which state of matter spreads out to fill its whole container?
solution: Gases (like the air inside a squad training ball) spread out to fill the space.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: Is the air inside a squad training ball matter?
answers: Yes. Air has mass and takes up space
solution: Air is matter! A pumped-up ball actually has a little more mass than a flat one.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: An ice cube melts into water. Did the type of matter change?
answers: No. It's still water, just in a different state
Yes. It became a new substance
solution: Melting is a physical change; it's still water.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: Your squad pours all the water from a shield-bottle prop into a wide bowl without spilling. Which property of the water stays the same?
solution: Liquids change shape but keep the same volume.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: MELTING is when…
answers: A solid turns into a liquid
A liquid turns into a gas
A gas turns into a liquid
A liquid turns into a solid
solution: Melting changes a solid into a liquid. For example, solid ice becomes liquid water; the substance remains water.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: FREEZING is when…
answers: A liquid turns into a solid
A solid turns into a liquid
A liquid turns into a gas
A gas turns into a solid
solution: Freezing changes a liquid into a solid. Liquid water becomes ice when enough heat is removed; it is still water.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: EVAPORATION is when…
answers: A liquid turns into a gas
A gas turns into a liquid
A solid turns into a liquid
A liquid turns into a solid
solution: Puddles disappear on sunny days because of evaporation.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: CONDENSATION is when…
answers: A gas turns into a liquid
A liquid turns into a gas
A solid turns into a gas
A liquid turns into a solid
solution: Water vapor in the air turns into liquid drops: condensation.
hint: Compare whether shape and volume stay fixed.

text: You want to know which material keeps a hot drink warm the longest. What should you measure?
answers: The temperature of each drink over time
solution: Track temperature with a thermometer to compare thermal insulators.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: To make a fair test comparing three cups, you should…
answers: Change only one thing and keep everything else the same
Use different amounts of water in each
Test each one on a different day
Change as many things as possible
solution: A fair test changes only ONE variable at a time.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: A student sorts objects into 'sticks to magnet' and 'doesn't stick.' What property is being used to classify them?
solution: Sorting by magnet = magnetism.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: Which set of tools would you need to find the mass AND volume of a liquid?
answers: A balance and a graduated cylinder
solution: Balance = mass. Graduated cylinder = volume.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: Why would a builder pick metal instead of plastic for an electrical wire?
solution: Wires need to conduct electricity, which metals do well.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: Which property would you test to choose the best material for an oven mitt?
solution: You want a material that blocks heat, which is low thermal conductivity.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: A team wants a cargo net that won't snap when a ball hits it. Which properties matter most?
solution: The net needs to stretch and not break.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: You want to build a supply raft that floats. What should you test?
answers: Whether the materials float or sink in water
solution: Floating vs. sinking is a property you can test with water.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: Why do scientists repeat an investigation several times?
answers: To make sure the results are reliable
solution: Repeating trials shows the results weren't just luck.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.

text: Inspect this mystery loot: it is shiny, silver-colored, attracted to a magnet, and conducts electricity. Which item best fits all four observations?
solution: Magnetic + conductor + shiny = steel. Aluminum conducts but ISN'T magnetic.
hint: Choose evidence for the property being tested. Keep other conditions the same.
